analysis.one_liner: Ends a major tax break that lets U.S. corporations delay paying tax on offshore profits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the tax code so that U.S. corporations pay tax on profits they book in foreign countries the same year they earn them, instead of being able to put off paying until the money is brought home. It would also block some large oil companies from using payments to foreign governments to reduce their U.S. tax bill, restrict interest deductions that let U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parent companies load up on debt here, treat foreign companies managed from the U.S. as domestic for tax purposes, and stop U.S. companies from avoiding U.S. tax by reincorporating abroad through a foreign merger (known as a corporate inversion).
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would share in billions of dollars of revenue if corporations that earn money in the U.S. system paid tax on their offshore profits and couldn't shrink their U.S. tax bill through foreign-debt stacking, foreign oil payments, or paper relocations abroad.

how_it_helps.text: It would eliminate the deferral of U.S. tax on the foreign-source income of U.S. corporations for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2015, so profits booked abroad would be taxed in the year earned rather than deferred. [S2]

It would deny the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies that are dual capacity taxpayers, so payments to foreign governments that come with a specific economic benefit could no longer be claimed as a credit against U.S. tax. [S2] [S3]
It would reinstate the per-country foreign tax credit, limiting the credit to income actually subject to U.S. tax. [S2] [S3]
It would treat foreign corporations that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for U.S. tax purposes. [S2] [S3]

It would restrict the interest deduction of U.S. members of financial reporting groups whose foreign common parent carries excess domestic indebtedness, curbing a common earnings-stripping technique. [S2] [S3]

It would revise inversion rules so that a foreign corporation acquiring a U.S. company or partnership after May 8, 2014 is treated as an inverted corporation — and taxed as domestic — if former U.S. owners hold more than 50% of the new entity. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-based multinational corporations (which would owe more current-year tax), large integrated oil companies (which would lose a foreign tax credit), foreign-domiciled corporate groups with U.S. subsidiaries (which would lose interest deductions), and companies attempting inversions. Some added compliance and competitive pressure would also fall on these firms and potentially on the U.S. workers and shareholders connected to them.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S. multinationals and large oil companies

drawbacks.text: Ending deferral entirely would tax foreign income in the year earned with no relief for taxes already paid abroad, a much harsher approach than the international systems used by peer countries, and could raise concerns about U.S. companies competing against foreign rivals. [S2] [S3]

The bill sets no explicit rate for taxing foreign income (it sweeps it into subpart F, which is taxed at regular corporate rates), so the practical impact on the deficit and on individual taxpayers would depend on how it were implemented. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an ambitious one: it attacks several of the most widely criticized corporate tax-avoidance channels at once — deferral, inversions, foreign oil payments, and earnings stripping. The cost is that it goes further than most international tax systems and may overreach by ending deferral outright rather than phasing in or pairing with rate relief, which is likely why it attracted no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never reported out or brought to the floor; it died at the end of the 114th Congress with zero cosponsors. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 14, 2015 by Rep. Janice Schakowsky (D-IL). [S1] [S5]
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is where it remained. [S5]
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup, vote, or floor vote in the 114th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations, large integrated oil companies, and companies seeking inversions are better off because the bill died: the current rules that allow deferral of offshore profits and other avoidance channels remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals that keep tax breaks intact

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never reported the bill out for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred and no cosponsors signed on, so partisan support cannot be measured from the record; the bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and no Republican backing.

industries.note: Would lose the ability to defer U.S. tax on profits booked in foreign countries, meaning more of their foreign earnings would be taxed each year. This matters because the deferred revenue is a share of the tax bill that ordinary taxpayers effectively absorb instead.

Would no longer be able to claim the foreign tax credit for payments to foreign governments that come with a specific economic benefit, reducing a tax benefit tied to the oil industry's overseas operations.

Mergers after May 8, 2014 that leave former U.S. owners holding more than 50% of the new foreign entity would be treated as domestic corporations for U.S. tax, removing a route to escaping U.S. tax on relocated companies.

industries.industry: Foreign-domiciled corporate groups with U.S. subsidiaries
industries.note: U.S. members of these groups would face a new cap on interest deductions, limiting a technique for shifting profits out of the U.S. tax base.
